result: The authors developed a novel experimental task that dissociates past (encoded location) and future (to-be-tested location) attributes of visual working memory by orthogonalizing these locations. Twenty-five participants memorized two colored gratings presented on orthogonal axes, with memory content always tested at a predictable location on the orthogonal axis.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised the experimental design. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'introduce an innovative twist' and 'disentangle the location where information is initially stored from the location where it will be tested.' Reviewer 3 notes the design 'neatly orthogonalized "past" and "future"' and calls it 'clever.' The editor affirms the study 'dissociates the locations during encoding and memory tests.'

result: After cue onset, saccades became biased toward the encoded (past) location of the selected memory target, starting around 200 ms after the cue. This reveals that retention of items in working memory continues to rely on their past encoded locations even when items are known to become relevant at another location. This past gaze bias replicates prior studies from the same lab.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 notes 'participants' gaze is biased towards the past encoding location, even though that location lacks relevance to the memory test.' Reviewer 3 states 'Figure 1b-d shows fairly clearly that saccade directions have an early peak (around 300ms) for the past.' The replication aspect is accepted without challenge.

result: A similar saccade bias toward the relevant future location was found, emerging early after the cue. This is the first demonstration of a bias to the future-relevant memory location that is similarly driven by microsaccades.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this novel finding. Reviewer 3 describes 'a "ramping" up of saccades moving in the forward direction' and notes the method can 'differentiate past from future oriented saccades.' Reviewer 2 highlights the observation of 'microsaccades directed towards both the past encoding location and the anticipated future test location' as 'noteworthy.'

result: The results reveal joint consideration of past and future locations, prevalent even at the single-trial level. Individual microsaccades showed dependency between past and future biases: the past bias was particularly pronounced for saccades that also had a future bias, and vice versa. Statistical analysis confirmed a clear interaction whereby the bias toward the future location was exclusively observed for saccades also biased toward the past location.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly endorse this central finding. Reviewer 3 states 'Figure 2, reveals a dependency in saccade direction such that saccades toward the probe future were more likely also to be toward the encoded location' and calls this 'persuasive evidence that past and future representations are jointly maintained.' Reviewer 2 describes the analysis as 'compelling' and notes it 'reveals the joint consideration of past and future locations during memory maintenance.'

result: The study unveils a novel, fundamental property of working memory: the joint availability and utilization of past and future memory attributes. The brain simultaneously retains copies of both past and future-relevant locations in working memory and (re)activates each during mnemonic selection. While it is not surprising that the future location is considered, it is far less trivial that both past and future attributes would be retained and (re)activated together.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as the central contribution. Reviewer 3 quotes the authors' characterization that 'the brain simultaneously retains the copy of both past and future-relevant locations in working memory' as the 'central contribution' and states the authors 'provide a nuanced analysis that offers persuasive evidence.' Reviewer 2 summarizes the work as presenting 'an innovative perspective on the adaptable nature of visual working memory.' The editor calls the study 'important' and states it 'advances our understanding.'

result: The discrete nature of saccades enabled demonstration of truly joint consideration of past and future attributes at the single-trial level, bypassing the fundamental challenge of disentangling multiple potential single-trial interpretations from trial-average data. Microsaccades are discrete events that allow tracking spatial attention at the single-trial level and serve as a promising complementary tool for uncovering mechanisms of spatial attention.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the methodological approach. Reviewer 3 notes the method 'can measure shifts of attention at a fine temporal resolution' and calls the gaze analyses 'state-of-the-art.' The editor describes the analyses as 'convincing' and 'state-of-the-art gaze analyses that build on a recent series of experiments introduced by the authors.' Reviewer 2 calls the analysis 'compelling.'

result: The data provide key support for the proposal that memory is fundamentally future-oriented, while also demonstrating that past memory attributes are not forgotten even when they do not become relevant again.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation without challenge. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'illustrate how information relevant to the future is integrated with past information to guide behavior.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the authors make 'remarks about the plausibility of various accounts of working memory encoding/maintenance' based on the findings. No reviewer questions this theoretical interpretation.

result: The authors considered whether memory contents could have been directly remapped to their future-relevant location, which would predict exclusively future-directed gaze bias. However, complementary analysis found no direct evidence for remapping in the period between encoding and cue.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this analysis or interpretation. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the authors make 'remarks about the plausibility of various accounts of working memory encoding/maintenance' and does not raise concerns about the remapping analysis. The finding is presented as supporting evidence against a pure remapping account.

result: Gaze biases in both axes were driven predominantly by microsaccades and occurred similarly in horizontal-to-vertical and vertical-to-horizontal trials. The past bias was relatively transient, while the future bias continued to increase in anticipation of the test stimulus and increasingly incorporated eye movements beyond the microsaccade range.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these characterizations of the temporal dynamics without challenge. Reviewer 3 describes the 'early peak (around 300ms) for the past' and 'ramping up of saccades moving in the forward direction,' which aligns with these claims. No reviewer questions the microsaccade-driven nature of the effects or the temporal patterns described.

result: Participants performed the dynamic visual working-memory task with an average accuracy of 70±2 percent correct and an average reaction time of 1218±125 ms.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the behavioral performance data. These basic performance metrics are accepted as demonstrating participants could perform the task. No concerns are raised about task difficulty or performance levels.

result: The future signal should be considered a content-specific memory attribute because the two memory contents were always associated with opposite testing locations, and the to-be-tested location was dependent on the item's encoding location regardless of its color. A critical difference with common pre-cue studies is that the cue never directly informed the relevant future location; rather, the future location was a feature of the cued memory item.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this logical inference from the experimental design without challenge. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the design 'neatly orthogonalized "past" and "future"' and does not question the content-specific nature of the future signal. The distinction from pre-cue studies is accepted as a key design feature.

result: The authors speculate on possible explanations for why past locations are retained: participants may have started but not finished dropping the past location, past locations may help individuate/separate memory items, or storing items with regard to multiple spatial frames may make memories more robust to decay and/or interference. The joint retention of multiple spatial attributes may make memories more robust and flexible for serving continuously evolving demands during everyday behavior.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these as reasonable speculations without challenge. These are clearly presented as interpretive possibilities rather than definitive conclusions. Reviewer 3 notes the authors make 'remarks about the plausibility of various accounts' and does not critique these speculative interpretations.

result: Working memory enables bridging past sensory information to upcoming future behavior and is concerned with two components: the past and the future. In conventional laboratory tasks, these components are often conflated, but in dynamic everyday situations, sensory information often disappears at one location but becomes relevant at another location.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this conceptual framing without challenge. These foundational claims about working memory and the motivation for the study are treated as established background. Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors 'delve into the link between anticipating future events and retaining previous visual information in memory.'
